{{short description|Canadian stem cell biologist}}
<!--needs infobox-->
[[File:Derrick Rossi 2.jpg|thumb|Derrick Rossi, 2008]]
'''Derrick J. Rossi''' (born 5 February 1966),<ref>''American Men & Women of Science'' (2015).  33rd Edition. Cengage Learning: Detroit.</ref> is a Canadian [[stem cell]] biologist and [[entrepreneur]]. He is a co-founder of the [[pharmaceutical]] company [[Moderna Therapeutics|Moderna]].

==Early life and education==
Rossi was born in Toronto as the youngest of five children of a [[Malta|Maltese]] immigrant family.<ref name=":nationalpost">{{ cite news |author=Joe O'Connor |url=https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/heroes-of-the-pandemic-meet-the-canadian-hockey-dad-behind-covid-19-vaccine-developer-moderna |title=Meet the Canadian hockey dad behind COVID-19 vaccine developer Moderna |work=nationalpost.com |date=28 May 2020| access-date =6 March 2021}}</ref> His father Fred worked in auto body shops for 50 years<ref>{{cite news |title=How Dad Made a Difference |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/268442399/?terms=Derrick%2BRossi |access-date=9 August 2018 |work=[[The Orlando Sentinel]] |date=16 June 2011 |page=D1 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> and his mother Agnes co-owned a Maltese bakery.<ref name=":nationalpost" />

Rossi attended the [[Dr Norman Bethune Collegiate Institute|Dr. Norman Bethune High School]] in [[Scarborough, Toronto|Scarborough]] where he early discovered his passion for [[molecular biology]].<ref name=":nationalpost" /> He then did his undergraduate and master's degrees in [[molecular genetics]] at the [[University of Toronto]].<ref name=":utoronto">{{cite web |author= Rahul Kalvapalle |url=https://www.utoronto.ca/news/lab-saving-lives-moderna-co-founder-derrick-rossi-becoming-serial-entrepreneur |title=From the lab to saving lives: Moderna co-founder Derrick Rossi on becoming a serial entrepreneur |work=utoronto.ca |date=22 February 2021 | access-date =6 March 2021}}</ref> He earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from the [[University of Helsinki]] in 2003 and held a [[Postdoctoral researcher|post-doc position]] from 2003 to 2007 at [[Stanford University]] in [[Irving Weissman]]’s lab.<ref name=":childrenshosp">{{cite web |url=https://www.childrenshospital.org/research/researchers/r/derrick-rossi |title=About the researcher |work=harvard.edu |date= |access-date=6 March 2021 |archive-date=9 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220209104526/https://www.childrenshospital.org/research/researchers/r/derrick-rossi |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career==
Rossi in 2007<ref>{{cite news|last=Anderson|first=Scott|date=9 June 2023|title=Derrick Rossi, the stem cell scientist who co-founded Moderna, receives honorary degree|url=https://www.utoronto.ca/news/derrick-rossi-stem-cell-scientist-who-co-founded-moderna-receives-honorary-degree|work=U of T News|publisher=University of Toronto|access-date=11 February 2025}}</ref> was appointed Associate Professor at the Stem Cell and Regenerative Biology Department at [[Harvard Medical School]] and [[Harvard University]].<ref name=":NYSCF">{{cite web|title=Derrick Rossi, PhD|url=https://nyscf.org/people/derrick-rossi-phd/|publisher=NYSCF|access-date=6 March 2021}}</ref> At the same time he was a principal faculty member of the Harvard Stem Cell Institute and an investigator at the Immune Disease Institute (IDI),<ref name="Research Gate">{{cite web|title=Derrick J Rossi's scientific contributionswhile affiliated with Harvard University (Cambridge, United States) and other places|url=https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/39287600_Derrick_J_Rossi|publisher=Research Gate|access-date=26 February 2018}}</ref> as well as in the Program in Cellular and Molecular Medicine at the [[Children’s Hospital Boston]].<ref name="VOR Biopharma">{{cite web|title=Derrick J. Rossi, Ph.D.|url=http://www.vorbiopharma.com/derrick-rossi/|publisher=VOR Biopharma|access-date=26 February 2018|archive-date=26 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180226152011/http://www.vorbiopharma.com/derrick-rossi/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Moderna was founded in 2010, based on discovery that [[pluripotent stem cells]] can be transformed and reprogrammed.<ref name="ekx">{{cite news |last1=Kutz |first1=Erin |title=ModeRNA, Stealth Startup Backed By Flagship, Unveils New Way to Make Stem Cells |url=https://xconomy.com/boston/2010/10/04/moderna-stealth-startup-backed-by-flagship-unveils-new-way-to-make-stem-cells/ |publisher=Xconomy, Inc |date=4 October 2010}}</ref><ref name=lgbe>{{cite web|author=Lawrence Goodman| url=https://www.brandeis.edu/now/2021/february/rosenstiel-ceremony-vaccine.html |title=Rosenstiel Award winners celebrated for life-saving scientific breakthroughs |work=brandeis.edu |date=10 February 2021 |access-date=6 March 2021}}</ref> ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine cited this pluripotent discovery as one of the top ten medical breakthroughs of the year.<ref name="Thriving">{{cite web|title=Children's researcher honored by TIME Magazine|url=https://thriving.childrenshospital.org/childrens-researcher-honnored-by-time-magazine/|publisher=Thriving|access-date=26 February 2018|archive-date=26 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180226211843/https://thriving.childrenshospital.org/childrens-researcher-honnored-by-time-magazine/|url-status=dead}}</ref> 

In 2013 Rossi, [[Kenneth R. Chien|Chien]] and their team reported that they "were able to improve heart function in mice and enhance their long-term survival with a "redirection of their [stem cell] differentiation toward cardiovascular cell types" in a significant step towards regenerative therapeutics for Moderna.<ref name="ltx">{{cite news |last1=Timmerman |first1=Luke |title=Moderna Vacuums Up Another $110M to Make Messenger RNA Drugs |url=https://xconomy.com/boston/2013/11/20/moderna-vacuums-another-110m-make-messenger-rna-drugs/ |publisher=Xconomy, Inc |date=20 November 2013}}</ref><ref name="chien13">{{Cite Q|Q30580723}}</ref> In the same year and on the strength of the same paper Moderna was able to partner with [[AstraZeneca]] in exchange for $240 million "in upfront cash (plus much more in potential milestone payments)", and then received from other investors $110 million.<ref name=ltx/>

In 2014 Rossi retired from his functions at the board and as a scientific advisor at Moderna.<ref name=":nationalpost" />

In 2015 Rossi was scientific co-founder of [[Intellia Therapeutics]]. In 2016 Rossi co-founded Magenta Therapeutics.<ref name=":utoronto" /> Rossi was involved in the foundation of Stelexis Therapeutics in 2017,<ref>{{cite news|date=7 January 2019|title=Stelexis Therapeutics Closes $43M in Series A Funding|url=https://www.finsmes.com/2019/01/stelexis-therapeutics-closes-43m-in-series-a-funding.html|work=FinSMEs|access-date=11 February 2025}}</ref> which develops new medication for treating cancerous stem cells.<ref name=":NYSCF" /><ref name=":utoronto" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Servick |first1=Kelly |title=This mysterious $2 billion biotech is revealing the secrets behind its new drugs and vaccines |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/mysterious-2-billion-biotech-revealing-secrets-behind-its-new-drugs-and-vaccines |access-date=9 August 2018 |work=Science |date=1 February 2017 |language=en}}</ref>

In 2018 Rossi retired from all of his Harvard positions in order to focus on his activities as an entrepreneur.<ref name=":utoronto" /><ref name=":nationalpost" /> Rossi served as the interim CEO of the [[New York Stem Cell Foundation]] from October 2022 to January 2024.<ref name=":NYSCF" /> Rossi is also CEO of [[Convelo Therapeutics]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nyscf.org/resources/the-science-of-startups-drs-derrick-rossi-and-paul-tesar-discuss-how-their-biotechs-are-bringing-stem-cell-research-to-patients/|title=The Science of Startups: Drs. Derrick Rossi and Paul Tesar Discuss How Their Biotechs Are Bringing Stem Cell Research to Patients|access-date=Dec 10, 2020}}</ref>

==Scientific contributions==
Rossi develops and promotes new therapies using biotechnological methods thus contributing to novel approaches in [[regenerative medicine]].<ref name=":NYSCF" /> His research focussed on different aspects of stem cell biology.<ref name=":utoronto" /> In order to avoid ethical issues related to the use and exploitation of human stem cells, Rossi based his developments on the results of [[Katalin Karikó]] and [[Drew Weissman]] on [[mRNA]]. He succeeded in finding investors for his plans to transfer these findings into new medications and vaccinations by founding Moderna.<ref>{{cite news |author=Damian Garde, Jonathan Saltzman |url=https://www.statnews.com/2020/11/10/the-story-of-mrna-how-a-once-dismissed-idea-became-a-leading-technology-in-the-covid-vaccine-race/ |title=The story of mRNA: How a once-dismissed idea became a leading technology in the Covid vaccine race |work=statnews.com |date=10 November 2020 |access-date=6 March 2021}}</ref>

Rossi is on record as writing of his synthetic modified mRNA: "because our technology is [[RNA]] based, it completely eliminates the risk of [[genomic integration]] and [[insertional mutagenesis]] inherent to all DNA-based methodologies."<ref name=rossi10a>{{Cite Q|Q28131663}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
In 2021 he was awarded the [[Princess of Asturias Awards|Princess of Asturias Award]] in the category "Scientific Research".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fpa.es/en/princess-of-asturias-awards/laureates/2021-katalin-kariko-drew-weissman-philip-felgner-ugur-sahin-ozlem-tureci-derrick-rossi-and-sarah-gilbert.html?especifica=0&idCategoria=0&anio=2021&especifica=0|title=Katalin Karikó, Drew Weissman, Philip Felgner, Uğur Şahin, Özlem Türeci, Derrick Rossi and Sarah Gilbert - Laureates - Princess of Asturias Awards|first=Developed with webControl CMS by Intermark|last=IT|website=The Princess of Asturias Foundation|accessdate=13 December 2021}}</ref>

==Family life==
Rossi is married to [[Finland|Finnish]] [[biologist]] Nina Korsisaari and father of three daughters.<ref name=":nationalpost" /><ref>{{cite news |author= Courtney Shea |url=https://torontolife.com/city/its-likely-well-see-another-pandemic-in-the-next-20-years-the-toronto-scientist-who-invented-the-covid-vaccine-technology-says-we-need-to-prepare-for-the-next-virus/ |title="It's likely we'll see another pandemic in the next 20 years": The Toronto scientist who invented the Covid vaccine technology says we need to prepare for the next virus|work=torontolife.com |date=17 February 2020 | access-date =6 March 2021}}</ref>
